analysis.one_liner: Lets bank companies own securities underwriting firms under strict limits, and requires clear account fee disclosure.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship on January 31, 1989, the bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have torn down part of the Glass-Steagall wall separating banking from the securities business, letting bank holding companies own firms that underwrite and trade stocks and bonds — while banning mergers between the largest banks and largest securities firms, building firewalls between banks and their securities affiliates, and holding back stock underwriting until Congress voted again. It paired that opening with real consumer protections: ads and mailings would have to clearly state interest yields, fees, and penalties, "free" accounts could not carry hidden fees, and banking regulators would get stronger enforcement powers. It also kept banks out of most insurance sales. The bill went nowhere after its first day.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank holding companies gain the right to own securities affiliates that underwrite, trade, and broker stocks and bonds — though banks with over $30 billion in assets are barred from merging with securities firms over $15 billion — plus faster regulatory approvals, municipal bond underwriting for national banks, and a new "diversified financial holding company" status exempt from some Federal Reserve oversight. Savers gain plain-language disclosure of yields, fees, and account terms, and regulators gain stronger tools to punish misbehaving banks. Independent insurance agents gain because the bill keeps bank holding companies out of most insurance sales.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals two Glass-Steagall provisions and lets bank holding companies acquire securities affiliates that underwrite, distribute, and deal in securities of any type, with Federal Reserve approval.

Requires banks to disclose savings account yields, minimum balances, and fees in plain language, bars advertising accounts as 'free' when they carry fees, and gives customers 30 days' notice before terms worsen.

Strengthens enforcement: banking agencies can issue temporary cease-and-desist orders, punish violations of written conditions, and penalize banks and individuals for hiring convicted felons, with penalties surviving a wrongdoer's resignation.
Speeds up the approval process: securities-affiliate applications not acted on within 91 days are deemed granted, and merger waiting periods can shrink to as little as 5 days.
Authorizes national banks without securities affiliates to underwrite municipal revenue bonds, sponsor unit investment trusts, and distribute mutual fund shares.
Creates 'diversified financial holding companies' that escape some Federal Reserve examination and capital requirements as long as banks stay under 20% of their assets.

analysis.who_pays: The federal deposit insurance system — backed ultimately by taxpayers — would stand behind companies combining insured banks with securities risk, which is the trade the bill's firewalls tried to manage but could not eliminate. Independent securities firms would face new competition from bank-owned affiliates, and federal regulators would take on heavy new coordination duties across five agencies. State laws barring bank–securities affiliations would be overridden.

drawbacks.text: Moving securities underwriting inside companies that own FDIC-insured banks puts securities risk closer to the federal deposit-insurance safety net that taxpayers backstop; the bill's firewalls (credit limits, no guarantees to affiliates, disclosure rules) aim to contain this but no wall is airtight.
The bill preempts state laws that prohibit banks from affiliating with securities firms, overriding stricter state-level protections.
The speed provisions cut both ways: applications deemed granted after 91 days and merger waiting periods as short as 5 days reduce the public's chance to weigh in on bank combinations.

Its protection for consumers who buy investments through banks rests mainly on disclosure — notices that securities are not deposits and are not FDIC-insured — which depends on customers reading and understanding them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer disclosure and enforcement titles are concrete, low-risk gains for anyone with a bank account, and the bill was drafted as a managed opening rather than a giveaway — with a ban on the biggest bank–securities firm mergers, real firewalls, capital conditions, and a delay on stock underwriting pending a later congressional vote. But the bill's center of gravity is the Glass-Steagall repeal, and the core tradeoff is unavoidable: securities losses inside a company that owns insured banks can seep toward the deposit insurance fund no matter how many walls are built. As drafted, the safeguards were unusually serious for a financial modernization bill, but the downside risk would have landed on the public's insurance system while the new profits flowed to bank holding companies.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never reported it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Dixon introduced the bill on January 31, 1989, joined by Senators Garn, Graham, and Wirth as original sponsors; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs that same day.
Five additional senators cosponsored the bill — 3 of 55 Senate Democrats and 2 of 45 Senate Republicans.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill sat in committee until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent Wall Street securities firms kept the underwriting business free of bank competition a while longer, and the deposit insurance fund avoided new securities risk; savers, however, went without the bill's fee-disclosure protections until Congress passed a separate truth-in-savings law in 1991.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent securities firms; deposit fund spared risk

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — two Democrats and two Republicans originally sponsored the bill and its five later cosponsors split 3 Democrats to 2 Republicans — but no vote was ever taken, so the chamber's actual alignment is unknown.

industries.note: The bill hands bank holding companies their long-sought prize: the right to own securities underwriting and brokerage affiliates, plus faster approvals and a lighter-touch holding company category. In exchange they accept firewalls, capital conditions, a ban on the largest bank–securities firm mergers, and near-total exclusion from insurance.

Bank-owned affiliates would bring new competition for underwriting and brokerage business, but the bill also outlaws mergers between the biggest banks and biggest securities firms and leaves Wall Street free to sell itself to smaller banking companies.

Title VII bars bank holding companies from insurance activities except narrow credit-related and small-town cases, insulating independent agents from bank competition — a win for the industry that comes from keeping an alternative sales channel closed to consumers.

Banks without securities affiliates may sponsor unit investment trusts and distribute fund shares, opening a huge new distribution channel, while the bill adds conflict-of-interest rules and bars funds from implying FDIC insurance.

Securities affiliates may not deal in asset-backed securities from their own banks unless the securities carry a rating from a nationally recognized rating organization, making agency ratings a legal requirement.
